text: Chun-Chuan Lin
Designed a trust layer for how Rightmove matches agents with consumers
A self-directed concept — replacing a checklist where every option is already paid for with a transparent, two-sided ranking flow, without breaking the business model underneath it.
Nov 2026 | Self-directed concept — flow audit, product strategy, coded prototype
Summary

Rightmove's agent-valuation flow promises a visit “from the local property experts you choose”, then hands you a checklist where every box is already ticked and every name on it paid to be there. I used that gap to explore what a Lead role on Rightmove's Partners domain actually requires.

item: 🔗 Diagnosed from both sides
Consumers get no trust signal. Agents get no way to differentiate beyond ad spend.
⚖️ Three directions weighed
Compared against two rejected alternatives, for stated reasons, before committing.
🧩 A flow, not a screen
Five seller screens and three agent screens, built as a prototype you can click through.
💷 Commercial model preserved
Paid placement stays. It just stops pretending to be a trust signal.

text: Role: self-directed, solo. Based on Rightmove's public pages — no internal data, no claim that this is what Rightmove is building.
The Problem
I walked the live flow on my own phone before drawing anything, following the in-home valuation path.

cap: rightmove.co.uk/agent-valuation, captured Nov 2026. Screens 3–5 are one page: by the time the agent list scrolls into view, every box is already ticked.

item: 🔗 Consumer side — a false choice
Every agent pre-ticked, every one Sponsored, nothing to tell them apart.
💷 Agent side — pay or disappear
The only differentiation on offer is paid placement. There's no non-paid tier to fall back on.

cap: Not a mockup — the final step, as shipped. Six agents, all Sponsored, all pre-ticked before you've read a single name.

text: Neither side gets a real trust mechanism — precisely the gap the job description names: “helping consumers feel more confident when choosing an estate agent, while helping agents demonstrate the value they offer.”
Alternatives Considered
Two genuinely different directions, not variations on one idea — so the choice would be a real trade-off.

cap: Three directionally different concepts, mapped against the same four questions.

dd: I chose the hybrid ranking — not because it scored best on every axis, but because it's the only one of the three that ships in phases and can be validated at low risk. Transparency-first's best property got folded in anyway: the Quality Score's methodology is published and queryable by agents.

text: The Approach
Paid decides where you're seen. It shouldn't decide why you're trusted — so the fix ships in phases, not one release.

item: 🚦 Phase 1 — Stop the list being 100% paid
Rightmove already labels this Sponsored. What's missing is a non-paid tier to label it against — and boxes that aren't pre-ticked by default.
📈 Phase 2 — Add a second, earned axis
Non-paid performance signals — time-to-sale, accuracy, response time — give agents without ad budget somewhere to compete.
🎯 Phase 3 — Let the two axes reward each other
Agents above a quality threshold get a lower cost-per-lead — both sides now have a reason to perform.

text: The Prototype
Not one screen — the whole decision, end to end, built in code so it can be clicked rather than just looked at.
One rule kept it simple: each screen answers one question. Who? Why them? Who else? Who gets my number?

cap: The seller's flow, recorded from the working prototype.
Five screens replace one pre-ticked page. Postcode and valuation type stay exactly as they are today.

text: 1 · A recommendation, not a checklist

item: 🎯 One agent, one button
Most sellers should be done here. Choosing takes a single tap.
🧭 Reasons in plain words
Flats like yours sold nearby, the price they get, how fast. No jargon, no star ratings, no explaining the design to the seller.
🚦 Nothing pre-ticked
No agent receives anything until the seller picks one — and the screen doesn't need to say so.

text: 2 · A score you can question

item: 📊 Three signals, plain words
Price, speed, replies — the same three things the agent sees about themselves.
⚖️ Paid is labelled, not hidden
A sponsored agent's sheet shows where it ranks on performance alone.

text: 3 · Compare is optional, and Sponsored stays honest

item: 💷 Sponsored keeps the top slot
Labelled, scored like everyone else, and shown with the rank it earns without paying.
🎚️ Re-sort, pick up to three
Fewer, deliberate requests — each one means something to the agent who gets it.

text: 4 · Details last, consent spelled out

item: 🔗 Choose first, then share
Today the phone number is typed in before the agent list appears.
🧑‍⚖️ Names who gets them
The consent line and the button both name exactly who receives the request.

text: The agent side — the same score, seen from the other end
A two-sided redesign that only shows the consumer screen hasn't solved the two-sided problem.

cap: Value Profile — one score, the one thing to fix, and what fixing it does to rank.
Leads — each one says how the seller found the agent, and that the request went to 2 agents rather than 6.
Placement — the top slot is still for sale; a higher score makes it cheaper. Pricing is illustrative.

text: Leading This
What I'd put on the table with the team before anyone built anything:

item: 🧭 With Research & Data
Rewarding valuation accuracy could reward conservative estimates over flattering ones. A history-based score also disadvantages the new, small agents the job is meant to help.
⚖️ With Commercial & Legal

A request sent to 2 chosen agents instead of 6 pre-ticked ones means fewer leads per paying agent. The bet — a chosen lead is worth more than a broadcast one — is Revenue's to test. Ranking also makes Rightmove an endorser, not a directory.
🎯 My own call to defend
Not building this as a Yelp-style comparison page — the valuation flow is a lead-gen funnel. One clear recommendation by default; comparison stays opt-in.

text: Reflection
This is a concept, not a validated design. The problem is real; the solution hasn't been in front of a single consumer or agent.

bullets: Put the prototype in front of sellers against the live pre-ticked flow — measure completion, not preference
Validate the Quality Score formula against real agent performance before trusting it to rank anyone
Pressure-test the pricing model with the team that owns Premium Listing revenue
Check whether “performance over reviews” holds once agents optimise for the metric itself

text: Why this belongs in the portfolio

Every other case study here is proof of execution on a real team. This one is proof of something else: given a problem I don't have internal access to, can I diagnose it accurately, generate real alternatives, and argue for a direction while being honest about where it could still go wrong.
